a community arts centre. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

Emily: [warm, friendly smile in voice] Good morning, Riverside Community Arts Centre. Emily speaking. How can I
help?
Daniel: [hesitant, a little unsure] Hi. Um… I'm calling because I'm interested in taking one of your evening art
classes.
Emily: [curious, genuinely interested] Certainly. We've got quite a few courses at the moment. Is there a particular
type of art you're interested in?
Daniel: [thoughtful, weighing it up] Hmm… well, I've always liked drawing, but I haven't really done anything
since school.
Emily: [reassuring, putting them at ease] Oh, that's absolutely fine. Our beginner drawing course is designed for
people with very little recent experience.
Daniel: [agreeing, nodding along] Oh, that's good.
Emily: [clear, matter-of-fact] The course covers basic sketching, perspective and observational drawing.
Daniel: [curious, leaning in] Okay. And when does it take place?
Emily: [clear, confident and precise] It's normally on Wednesday evenings, from six thirty until eight thirty.
Daniel: [considering, thoughtful pause] Wednesday could work for me.
Emily: [practical, helpful tone] We also have a Saturday morning course, although… um, that's currently full.
Daniel: [quick, energetic] Ah, right.
Emily: [reassuring, gentle and calm] We do have a waiting list for the Saturday class, though.
Daniel: [considering, mulling it over] I think Wednesday would probably be easier anyway.
Emily: [warm, welcoming] Excellent. The next course starts in October.
Daniel: [curious, genuinely interested] How much does it cost?
Emily: [clear, matter-of-fact] The full six-week course is ninety pounds.

Emily: [practical, efficient] Materials aren't included, but you don't need to buy everything before the
first class.
Daniel: [hesitant, searching for words] So… what would I need to bring?
Emily: [warm, genuinely pleased] I'll explain that, as well as the registration arrangements, in a moment.

NARRATOR: Section 4. You will hear part of a university lecture about how plants adapt to dry
environments. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.
Test1_Sec4_Full_Voice.mp3
Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon. Today we're going to examine how plants survive in dry
environments and the different adaptations that allow them to cope with limited water.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Water is essential for plants because it is involved in photosynthesis, nutrient
transport and the maintenance of cell structure.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective pause] In dry environments, however, water may be unavailable for long
periods.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So, plants living in these conditions have evolved a range of physical and
physiological adaptations.
Lecturer: [clear, confident and precise] One of the most obvious adaptations is a reduction in water loss.
9
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Plants lose water mainly through tiny openings in their leaves called stomata.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, considering carefully] Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis, but
they can also allow water vapour to escape.
Lecturer: [measured, deliberate pacing] Many plants adapted to dry environments therefore have mechanisms
that reduce the amount of water lost through these openings.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Some species can close their stomata during particularly hot or dry periods.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective pause] Another adaptation involves the structure of the leaves themselves.
Lecturer: [clear, confident and precise] Some plants have small or narrow leaves, which reduces the surface area
through which water can be lost.
Lecturer: [confident, self-assured] Other species have thick leaves containing specialised tissues that can
store water.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Succulent plants are a familiar example.
Lecturer: [clear, confident and precise] Their fleshy leaves or stems can hold substantial quantities of water, allowing
the plant to survive periods when rainfall is limited.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, considering carefully] Root systems can also play an important role.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Some desert plants develop very deep roots that allow them to reach water
stored below the surface.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Others develop extensive shallow root systems.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, weighing it up] These can rapidly absorb water from the upper layers of soil after brief
rainfall.
Lecturer: [measured, calm authority] The choice between deep and shallow roots depends partly on the local
environment.
Lecturer: [clear, confident and precise] Temperature is another important factor.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective pause] High temperatures increase evaporation and can therefore make water
loss more rapid.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Some plants reduce their activity during the hottest part of the day.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Others may carry out a greater proportion of their gas exchange at night.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, considering carefully] This can reduce water loss because temperatures are lower and humidity
is often higher.
Lecturer: [clear, confident and precise] Plants can also modify their growth patterns.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In extremely dry conditions, some species grow very slowly.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective pause] Although slow growth limits the rate at which a plant becomes larger, it
also reduces the amount of water and energy required for new tissue.
Lecturer: [measured, deliberate pacing] These adaptations do not mean that dry-environment plants require no
water.
Lecturer: [reassuring, confident warmth] They simply allow plants to use limited water more efficiently and survive
longer periods of stress.
Lecturer: [reflective, musing] Climate change is making the study of these adaptations increasingly
important.
Lecturer: [measured, calm authority] Changes in rainfall patterns may expose plants to longer or more
unpredictable periods of drought.
Lecturer: [clear, steady] Understanding how plants respond to water stress can therefore help
10
researchers identify species that may be better suited to future environmental conditions.
Lecturer: [measured, deliberate pacing] At the same time, conservation remains important because plants cannot
always adapt quickly enough to major environmental changes.
Lecturer: [reflective, contemplative] Next week, we'll examine how plants compete for light in dense forest
ecosystems. Please read the section on plant competition before the next lecture.
Script QC
